The factors are per dollar of commodity output at producer price, in 2024 U.S. dollars, the model’s base year. They include every upstream supplier, but not the trade and transport services between the producer and the buyer, which are handled in

The release has a factor for each of 21 regions and one global average (
). For each sector and each gas, a regional factor is the average of its member countries’ factors, weighted by each country’s output of that sector in 2024 dollars (

Only countries in Tiers 0 to 2 have output data in the model, so Tier 3 countries are not included in the weighted average, even where they belong to the region. A region with no Tier 0 to 2 member uses the simple average of its members’ factors instead. The global average is weighted the same way over every Tier 0 to 2 country. The rest-of-world region is used only inside the model and is not published.

A few country–sector combinations have a total factor of exactly zero, because the source tables have no output or no emissions for that sector in that country. A zero factor would understate emissions for anyone buying from that sector, so it is treated as missing: the country’s factor is replaced by its region’s factor, or by the global average where the regional factor is also zero. The replacement applies to every gas.
From the base year to each reporting year
Every source in the model is first brought to 2024 dollars: values are converted to U.S. dollars at the data year’s exchange rate and re-priced to 2024 with a U.S. price index (see
). The model therefore produces 2024 factors, per 2024 dollar.
The factors for 2025 and 2026 are re-priced from the 2024 factors, sector by sector:
is the sector’s price index and

is the year. When a sector’s prices rise, each dollar buys less of its output, so the factor per dollar falls. The emissions behind the factors are the same; only the dollar they are expressed in changes. Each year’s factors are therefore in current dollars of that year.

The price index is the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis chain-type price index for gross output by industry (2017 = 100), mapped to the 405 sectors. The 2026 value is the average of the quarters published at the time of the release. Sectors without their own index keep a constant price. The same U.S. index is applied to every country, region and the global average.

A purchaser pays more than the producer receives: wholesale, retail and transport businesses add their margins on the way to the buyer. Each dollar at purchaser price therefore contains less of the product itself. The purchaser-price factor converts the producer-price factor to this larger dollar:

is the producer share of the purchaser price.

The conversion covers trade and transport margins. Taxes and subsidies on products are not included.
They carry no trade margins, so their producer- and purchaser-price factors are the same.
The margin coefficients are re-priced to each year with the price indexes of the margin sector and of the commodity, so
changes slightly from year to year.

The purchaser-price factor covers the emissions of making the product only. The emissions of the margin services themselves, such as running warehouses, stores and trucks, are not added to it; they are prepared as separate
Published factors are rounded to three significant figures. Total GHGs is rounded from the unrounded total, so it may not equal the sum of the rounded gas values.
2025 and 2026 factors reflect price changes only
The supply chains and emission intensities of the 2024 model also describe 2025 and 2026. The factors for those years differ from 2024 only by the change in each sector’s price.
Input-output tables and emissions data for 2025 and 2026 are not yet available for any country.
Real changes after 2024, such as a cleaner electricity grid or a shift in where inputs are bought, are not captured in the 2025 and 2026 factors.
One U.S. price index for every country
Each sector’s U.S. price change applies to that sector in every country.
Consistent sector-level price indexes in U.S. dollars are not available for every country and year.
Where prices in a country moved differently from U.S. prices, or its exchange rate against the dollar changed, its factors for 2025 and 2026 could be too high or too low.
U.S. margins and no product taxes in purchaser prices
The U.S. share of trade and transport margins in each commodity’s purchaser price applies in every country, and product taxes are left out of the conversion.
Margin and tax data comparable to the U.S. tables are not available for every country.
Where a country’s margins or product taxes differ from the U.S., its purchaser-price factors could be too high or too low. Producer-price factors are not affected.
A region’s factor for a sector is the average of its member countries’ factors weighted by their output of that sector, using only countries in Tiers 0 to 2.
Output is the best available measure of how much of a sector’s supply each country provides, and it is available only for countries with IO tables.

The regional factor reflects the region’s largest producers. Where a region’s Tier 3 members produce differently from its Tier 0 to 2 members, their purchases are better represented by their own country factors.
